slides.text: The case study Tilal Regional Tourism Board: three years, six tables 9 visitor sites in a highland region 150,000 ticket sales, 2023 to 2025 40,000 visitor stays in the register 6,000 survey responses, Arabic and English You work as Leen Al-Suwayigh, the board's analyst. Nawal Al-Rashoud, the director, wrote the brief. Aws Al-Hudaif runs sites and ticketing, Rashed Al-Shalan collects the hotels' occupancy returns, Atheer Al-Muhaya owns the survey and the complaints log, Nayef Al-Jumaah drew the charts of last year's report, Hanouf Al-Rumaihi is the data protection officer. slides.title: An answerable question names four things
slides.text: The tool of this session An answerable question names four things Part It says Ask 3, rewritten Unit of observation what one row is one complaint; one ticket sale Variables which columns are used site; tickets in the sale Comparison what is set against what complaints per thousand visitors, by site Kind exploring, or testing a claim fixed in advance exploratory The test. Could a colleague answer it without phoning you? "How many complaints per thousand visitors does each site receive?" passes. "Is it our problem site?" does not.

slides.title: "Visitors" is a different thing in every table
slides.text: What one row is "Visitors" is a different thing in every table Table One row is Rows arrivals one origin market in one month 180 tickets one ticket sale at one site 150,000 stays one visiting party's stay in the region 40,000 occupancy one hotel on one day 43,840 survey one visitor's response after a site visit 6,000 complaints one complaint 2,418 Counting rows counts units: 40,000 stays are parties, not people. Two tables meet only after both are brought to one unit, such as the week.

slides.title: Exploring finds questions; confirming answers one fixed in advance
slides.text: Two kinds of work Exploring finds questions; confirming answers one fixed in advance Exploratory You look at the data to see what is there Many cuts, many charts, the choice made after looking Output: patterns worth a question Honest wording: "we saw", "in this data" Confirmatory The comparison was written down before the data was seen One planned analysis on data not used to find the pattern Output: evidence for or against a claim Honest wording: "the test planned in advance showed" Why a found pattern needs a fresh test. The data that suggested a pattern cannot also confirm it: you chose the pattern because it stood out there.

slides.title: The plan is a table, and it passes a checklist
slides.text: One page before any chart The plan is a table, and it passes a checklist {"question": "How many complaints per thousand visitors does each site receive over the three years?", "table": "complaints", "also": ["tickets"], "unit": "one complaint logged by the visitor experience team", "variables": ["site", "tickets"], "comparison": "complaints per thousand visitors by site, with the count and the visitors beside it", "kind": "exploratory"} The checklist rejects a question with a word nobody can measure, a unit that is not the table's, fewer than two variables, or no comparison. It does not judge whether the question is interesting. That stays with you and the director.

slides.title: The plan answers "what happened", not "why"
slides.text: A narrower promise The plan answers "what happened", not "why" Ask 5: "Satisfaction went down last year. Why, and whose fault is it?" Plan: "Did mean satisfaction change from 2024 to 2025 inside each origin market, and did the mix of markets among respondents change?" The data can show where the fall sits. It cannot assign a cause: nothing was varied on purpose. Say so in the plan, before the director expects more.

slides.title: Which rewrite can be answered?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which rewrite can be answered? The director asks: "Did the festivals bring people, or would they have come anyway?" Which rewrite belongs in the plan? Were the festivals successful for the region? How many arrivals were recorded in the festival months? By how much did arrivals in each festival month exceed the baseline for that month of the year? Did the festivals cause visitors to choose Tilal over other regions?

slides.title: A profile asks six things of a table
slides.text: Before the first chart of a table A profile asks six things of a table 1 · Grain and key Is one row what the dictionary says? Is the key unique? 2 · Types Are dates dates and numbers numbers, or text that looks like them? 3 · Missing values How many, and above all where? 4 · Ranges Smallest and largest: can they be true? 5 · Categories How many distinct values, and how spelled? 6 · Coverage Which period and which groups does the table hold?

slides.title: 40,600 rows hold 40,000 stays
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 1 40,600 rows hold 40,000 stays 40,600 rows in the export 40,000 distinct stay keys 600 rows that repeat an earlier row in every column Every repeated key is an exact copy: a double entry, safe to drop. Had the copies differed in any column, the repair would be the owner's decision, not yours. Left in, the copies make every count 1.5% too high and nothing looks wrong.

slides.title: The share of missing values matters less than where they sit
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 2 The share of missing values matters less than where they sit Day visits 21.7% without spend Overnight stays 2.1% without spend Overall, spend is missing in 2,577 of 40,000 stays: 6.4%, which sounds harmless. Day visitors spend least and answer least. An average over the rows that remain leans toward overnight visitors. The decision: keep the rows, report the share missing by group, never fill in a typical value.

slides.title: A code that poses as a number moves every summary
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 3 A code that poses as a number moves every summary 11.26 mean nights with the 320 rows of 999 left in 3.30 mean nights without them 999 means "not recorded". It is in 0.8% of the rows and more than triples the mean. One market is stored as Gulf, GCC and gulf with a trailing space: 586 stays would fall out of any group-by. 14 stays arrive in 2032. Look at the smallest and the largest value of every column , and at every distinct value of a category with few of them.

slides.title: An issue log holds evidence and a decision someone can dispute

The supplied clean register, U.stays(), applies exactly these decisions, and every later lab starts from it.

slides.text: Checkpoint What do you do with the 999s? 320 stays have 999 in the column nights. The data dictionary does not mention the value. What goes into the issue log? slides.title: Distributions
slides.text: Session 3 Distributions Draw a histogram with a bin width that suits the variable Compare groups of unequal size by shares on a common scale Recognise a distribution with two humps that a box plot hides 03

slides.title: A distribution answers "which values, how often"
slides.text: One variable at a time A distribution answers "which values, how often" Lab 1.3, step 1: nights in the region, all parties, one bin per night. Read four things: where the bulk is, how wide, how many humps, how long the tail. Here: a spike at 0, a hump at 2, a low hump near 7, a tail to 31. Three humps in one histogram usually mean three kinds of unit mixed together.

slides.title: The bin width decides what a histogram can show
slides.text: The one choice a histogram has The bin width decides what a histogram can show Too wide Bins of 7 nights put 13,205 of the 17,367 stays from other regions into the first bar. Two humps become one. Fitted to the variable Nights is a count: one bin per night. Spend spans three orders of magnitude: equal steps on a log scale. Too narrow Bins of 10 riyals of spend leave a handful of stays in each bar: the shape drowns in noise. Try two or three widths and keep the one where the shape stops changing. Say the width in the axis title or the caption.

slides.title: To compare groups of unequal size, compare shares
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 2 To compare groups of unequal size, compare shares Counts would show the size of each market, not its shape. 80% of parties from the Tilal region are day visits; none from Europe. "Other regions" has two humps with nothing at 4 nights.

slides.title: A box plot draws five numbers and takes one line per group
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 3 A box plot draws five numbers and takes one line per group The same stays as the five histograms. Box: first quartile, median, third quartile. Whiskers: the rest, short of far points. Good for many groups and for comparing middles and spreads. "Other regions" and "Asia" look alike here: medians 3 and 4, boxes 2 to 6 and 2 to 5.

slides.title: The box cannot show two humps
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 4 The box cannot show two humps Nights, "Other regions" 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Share of stays 15% 31% 16% 0% 4% 10% 10% 7% 4% 63% of these stays last 1 to 3 nights and 37% last 5 or more. None lasts 4. The median, 3 nights, belongs to the short trips only. The box, 2 to 6, runs straight across the valley. The box plot is not wrong. It was asked "what kinds of trip are there" and answers "where is the middle half".

slides.title: Smooth curves and small groups both invent detail
slides.text: Two cautions Smooth curves and small groups both invent detail Density curves A density plot is a smoothed histogram with a bandwidth in place of a bin width. It overlays well, and it draws mass where no value can be: below zero nights, between whole nights. For counts and scores, prefer bars. Small groups A histogram of 40 values has bumps that mean nothing. Read a group's size before its shape: Europe has 2,166 stays here, one site in one month may have a dozen. Responsible use. A point drawn for one extreme party can single out an identifiable visitor. Show far points only where a group is large, or summarise them.

slides.title: Which chart for which question?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which chart for which question? Aws Al-Hudaif asks whether visitors from other regions come for one kind of trip or several. You have their 17,367 stays with the nights of each. What do you draw first? A box plot of nights for that market A bar with the mean number of nights and an error bar A histogram of nights with bins seven nights wide A histogram of nights with one bin for each night

slides.title: Summaries that fit the shape
slides.text: Session 4 Summaries that fit the shape Predict from mean and median which way a variable is skewed Choose a centre and a spread that the tail does not move Summarise a zero-heavy variable and a score without a single mean 04

slides.title: The gap between mean and median is a first reading of the shape
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 1 The gap between mean and median is a first reading of the shape Variable Mean Median Mean / median Spend per party, riyals 2,736 1,498 1.83 Nights 3.30 2 1.65 Booking lead, days 16.2 6 2.70 Satisfaction, 1 to 5 4.12 4 1.03 A mean far above the median says "long right tail" before any chart is drawn. Mean and median that agree do not prove symmetry: satisfaction is piled against the top of its scale.

slides.title: "Mean plus or minus one standard deviation" can describe nobody
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 2 "Mean plus or minus one standard deviation" can describe nobody Spend, as often reported 2,736 ± 3,788 riyals. The lower end is 1,051 riyals below zero. No party spent that. Spend, by quartiles Median 1,498; half of the parties between 571 and 3,392. Three amounts that real parties spent. The standard deviation squares distances, so a few large bills dominate it. Removing the top 1% of spend cuts the standard deviation by 24% and the median by 1.5%.

slides.title: Variables that multiply are symmetric on a log scale
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 3 Variables that multiply are symmetric on a log scale Spend per party, equal steps on a log scale. Spend is nights times party size times a daily rate. On a log scale, equal distances are equal ratios. Geometric mean 1,344 riyals: near the median 1,498, half the mean 2,736.

slides.title: A zero-heavy variable needs two numbers
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 4 A zero-heavy variable needs two numbers 36% of parties did not book at all: lead time 0 14 days median lead of those who booked 6 days median of everyone, which describes neither group Two populations share one column: walk-ins and bookers. First the share at zero, then a summary of the rest. The same shape: spend on tickets among all residents, complaints per visitor, days absent.

slides.title: A score from 1 to 5 is summarised by shares
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 5 A score from 1 to 5 is summarised by shares 5 39.2% 4 38.3% 3 18.1% 2 4.1% 1 0.4% "77% score 4 or 5" is a sentence a board can repeat. "Mean 4.12" hides whether the rest are at 3 or at 1. A mean of scores assumes the step from 4 to 5 equals the step from 1 to 2. It is still used to compare groups, as Day 2 will; show the shares beside it.

slides.title: Every question gets a chart, a summary and two sentences
slides.text: The evidence for outcome 3 Every question gets a chart, a summary and two sentences Shape Centre Spread Chart Long right tail (spend) median, or geometric mean quartiles histogram on a log scale Count with humps (nights) median, with the share in each hump shares by range bars, one per value Zero-heavy (booking lead) share of zeros, median of the rest quartiles of the rest two parts Score (satisfaction) share scoring 4 or 5 all five shares bars of shares A summary always carries the number of values it rests on and what was left out: here the 2,577 stays with no stated spend, most of them day visits.

slides.text: Day 1 Three things to keep The question comes first Unit of observation, variables, comparison, and whether you are exploring or confirming. slides.title: Which summary would you send the director?
slides.text: Review · Day 1 Which summary would you send the director? Spend per stay has a mean of 2,736 riyals and a median of 1,498. It is missing for 22% of day visits and 2% of overnight stays. Which sentence is honest? A typical party spends about 2,700 riyals in the region Half of the parties that reported spend spent under 1,500 riyals; day visits are under-reported Spend is about 1,500 riyals once missing values are filled in Spend cannot be summarised until the largest stays are removed

slides.title: Two variables at once
slides.text: Session 1 Two variables at once Bring two tables to one unit of observation before relating them Reveal a relation in an overplotted scatter with transparency and binning Explain why a correlation changes with the unit it is computed on 01

slides.title: Two tables relate only at one unit of observation
slides.text: Before two variables can meet Two tables relate only at one unit of observation tickets 150,000 sales, summed to tickets per day + occupancy 43,840 hotel-days, rooms sold over rooms → one table 43,840 rows: a hotel, a day, its occupancy, the day's tickets Bring each table to the unit of the answer, then join. Count the rows before and after. More rows: something was repeated. Fewer: something was dropped. The day's ticket total is repeated on 40 hotels. That is intended, and it has a consequence you will see.

slides.title: 43,840 opaque points draw a block, not a relation
slides.text: The first attempt 43,840 opaque points draw a block, not a relation Every point is there. Nothing can be read. A scatter plot shows each unit as a point. Past a few thousand, points hide points. The block says only where data exists: 152 to 836 tickets a day, 0 to 100% of rooms. Overplotting hides density, and density is the message.

slides.title: Transparency turns overlap into darkness
slides.text: Repair 1 · Lab 2.1, step 2 Transparency turns overlap into darkness The same points at opacity 0.04. A dark band now rises from left to right. The horizontal stripes are banding: a hotel of 8 rooms can only be 0, 1/8, 2/8 … full, nine possible values. Banding is a feature of the unit, not of tourism. Name it so that nobody explains it. alt.Chart(hd).mark_circle(size=8, opacity=0.04).encode(x="tickets_day:Q", y="rate:Q")

slides.title: Bin both axes and colour by count
slides.text: Repair 2 · Lab 2.1, step 3 Bin both axes and colour by count A histogram in two dimensions. Each cell counts the hotel-days that fall in it. The count goes to colour. It works for a million points as well as for forty thousand. It shows where the points are. It does not yet say how much occupancy rises.

slides.title: To read "how much", summarise y inside bins of x
slides.text: Repair 3 · Lab 2.1, step 4 To read "how much", summarise y inside bins of x Eight groups of days, equal in size, by tickets sold. Cut the days into eighths by tickets sold; take the median occupancy of each. Quietest eighth: 40% of rooms sold. Busiest eighth: 77%. The y axis runs from 0 to 100%, so the rise is drawn at its true size.

slides.title: One relation, two units, two correlations
slides.text: Lab 2.1, step 5 One relation, two units, two correlations 0.39 across 43,840 hotel-days 0.70 across 156 weeks, all hotels together Adding up 40 hotels and 7 days averages away what is particular to one hotel on one night. Weeks answer: does the region's occupancy move with the sites? Hotel-days answer: can one hotel's night be told from the day's ticket sales? There is no "the correlation". Report the coefficient with its unit and its number of units.

slides.title: A relation between two series is not yet a reason
slides.text: The second sentence of the reading A relation between two series is not yet a reason Summer raises ticket sales. Summer raises hotel bookings. Festivals do the same, in October and February. Two series that share a calendar move together whether or not one feeds the other. What the reading may say "Weeks with more ticket sales are weeks with fuller hotels (0.70 across 156 weeks). Both rise in summer and at festivals, so the data does not show that site visits fill hotels."

slides.title: Counts, rates and denominators
slides.text: Session 2 Counts, rates and denominators Convert counts to rates with a denominator that fits the question Compare a ranking by count with a ranking by rate Mark the cells of a table that a publication rule holds back 02

slides.title: A ranking by count is mostly a ranking by size
slides.text: Ask 3 of the brief A ranking by count is mostly a ranking by size Site Complaints Visitors Cable Car 599 100,822 Souq Walk 394 77,599 Tilal Fort 296 53,558 Wadi Trail 243 21,408 Terrace Farms 167 12,083 "A lot of complaints about the Cable Car": 599 of 2,418, a quarter of the log. It also receives a quarter of all visitors. The count answers "where is the workload?". It does not answer "where does a visit go wrong most often?".

slides.title: The denominator is whoever could have produced the event
slides.text: The choice that decides the answer The denominator is whoever could have produced the event Question Rate Denominator Where does a visit go wrong most often? complaints per thousand visitors tickets sold at the site Which market complains most readily? complaints per thousand visitors of that origin tickets sold to that origin Is the queue the issue on busy days? queue complaints per thousand visitors, by day tickets sold that day Per thousand, so that the reader sees numbers like 5.9, not 0.0059. A rate travels with its two parts: 599 of 100,822.

slides.title: Bring each table to the unit of the answer, then join
slides.text: Lab 2.2, step 2 Bring each table to the unit of the answer, then join WITH c AS (SELECT site, count(*) AS complaints FROM complaints GROUP BY site), v AS (SELECT site, sum(tickets) AS visitors FROM tickets GROUP BY site) SELECT site, complaints, visitors, 1000.0 * complaints / visitors AS per_thousand FROM c JOIN v USING (site) ORDER BY per_thousand DESC Nine rows in, nine rows out. The totals still read 2,418 complaints and all tickets sold. Joining the raw tables on site pairs every complaint with every sale: millions of rows and a rate that means nothing.

slides.title: By rate, the Cable Car is fifth and the smallest site is first
slides.text: Lab 2.2, step 3 By rate, the Cable Car is fifth and the smallest site is first Complaints per thousand visitors, 2023 to 2025. Cable Car: first by count, fifth by rate (5.9). Terrace Farms: seventh by count, first by rate (13.8), on 167 complaints. Wadi Trail is high on both readings of "problem": fourth by count (243), second by rate (11.4).

slides.title: Cut finer and the highest rates rest on the fewest cases
slides.text: Lab 2.2, steps 4 and 5 Cut finer and the highest rates rest on the fewest cases Site × origin Complaints Visitors Published Terrace Farms × Asia 6 441 withheld Terrace Farms × Europe 4 321 withheld Cloud Lookout × Asia 6 1,769 withheld Honey Museum × Asia 8 2,075 withheld The board's rule: publish a cell only with at least 10 complaints and 1,000 visitors. Four of 45 cells are held back. Two of them would have shown the highest rates in the table. One more complaint moves a rate built on 4 by a quarter.

slides.title: A withheld cell beside a published total can be recovered
slides.text: The stretch of lab 2.2 A withheld cell beside a published total can be recovered By subtraction Honey Museum: 139 complaints in total, four origin cells published, one withheld. The fifth is 139 minus the four: 8. What the analyst does marks every cell that fails the rule checks each row and column for a single withheld cell hands the table to the person who owns the rule Where this continues. Second-cell suppression, differencing between releases and the classification of outputs are taught in DS-207. Here you learn to see the problem and to mark the cells.

slides.title: Which sentence can be printed?

slides.title: A total is a weighted average: the weights are the mix
slides.text: The mechanism A total is a weighted average: the weights are the mix overall mean = sum over groups of ( share of the group × mean of the group ) 2024: 0.40 × 4.50 + 0.35 × 4.20 + 0.12 × 3.70 + 0.07 × 3.41 + 0.06 × 3.30 = 4.15 2025: 0.26 × 4.60 + 0.30 × 4.30 + 0.19 × 3.80 + 0.13 × 3.49 + 0.12 × 3.41 = 4.07 The total moves when the group means move, or when the shares move. Here the means all rose by about 0.1 and the shares moved against them.

slides.title: Every chart is four decisions
slides.text: The grammar of graphics Every chart is four decisions Part The decision In lab 3.1 Data what one row is one site: complaints, visitors, rate Marks the shape drawn for each row a circle, a rule, a text Encodings which column drives which visual channel rate → x, site → y, visitors → size Scales how values become positions, sizes and colours x from zero; sites sorted by rate Why think this way. "Bar chart" and "scatter plot" are names for a few common combinations. The four parts describe all of them, and tell you what to change.

slides.title: Give the most precise channel to the comparison that matters
slides.text: Not all channels are read equally well Give the most precise channel to the comparison that matters Position on a common scale most precise Length Angle and slope Area Colour intensity least precise Colour hue tells categories apart; it does not order them. A small difference shows in position long before it shows in area or shade.

slides.title: The written specification and the code have the same four parts
slides.text: Lab 3.1, steps 2 and 3 The written specification and the code have the same four parts alt.Chart(rates).mark_circle().encode( # data, mark x=alt.X("per_thousand:Q", # encoding: a quantity scale=alt.Scale(zero=True), # scale: from zero title="Complaints per thousand visitors, 2023 to 2025"), y=alt.Y("site:N", sort="-x", title=None), # a name, sorted by x ).properties(title="Complaints per thousand visitors by site") :Q a quantity, :N a name, :O an order, :T a time. The type picks the default scale. Sorting and titles are part of the specification, not decoration.

slides.title: Layers share the data and the scales, and add one mark each
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 4 Layers share the data and the scales, and add one mark each Rule, circle and text: three layers. The rate has position; the visitors have area. The largest circle is fifth from the top. One chart now says what lab 2.2 needed a paragraph for. alt.layer(rule, dot, label)

slides.title: Change one part and you can say what was gained and lost
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 5 Change one part and you can say what was gained and lost The same data, x and y, as bars. A bar's length already carries the rate, so size is taken: the visitors drop off the chart. Bars are familiar and read fast. A bar is measured from its base. A point is read by its place. The rule that follows. Bars and areas need an axis from zero. Points and lines may use an axis that starts elsewhere, if the chart says so.

slides.text: Lab 3.2, step 2 Small multiples: the same chart, one panel per group One y scale for all panels. No legend: each panel is labelled. Once one panel is understood, all are. A shared scale compares levels across panels: who is big. Asia and Europe are still flat lines.

Free scales with no note. The reader compares heights across panels anyway and concludes that all markets are the same size.

slides.title: Small multiples trade exact comparison for clarity
slides.text: When panels stop helping Small multiples trade exact comparison for clarity They suit Three to about twenty groups; one simple chart repeated; a reader who compares patterns. They strain Two lines whose gap is the message: put those on one panel, where the gap has position. They need A deliberate order of panels, identical axes in type, and few tick labels on each. A useful middle way. Draw every group in grey in every panel and highlight one. The reader gets the shape and the place among the others.

slides.title: Six charts, every number correct, every impression wrong
slides.text: The board's earlier report Six charts, every number correct, every impression wrong Fault What it does Repair Cut baseline a bar's axis does not start at zero start at zero, or change the mark Picked window a few periods chosen out of many show the whole series Count for rate counts compared across unequal groups divide by the denominator Two axes two scales stretched until shapes agree one variable against the other Running total a cumulative line, which can only rise plot the amount per period Uneven steps unequal periods drawn as equal steps equal periods on a time axis

slides.title: "Satisfaction collapsed in 2025"
slides.text: Fault 1 · Cut baseline "Satisfaction collapsed in 2025" As published: the axis runs from 4.0 to 4.2. Repaired: bars from zero. A bar says "this much". Cut the base and the 2025 bar is half the 2024 bar for a fall of 2%. If 0.08 matters, use points on a stated axis, with intervals.

slides.title: "Arrivals up 37% in a year"
slides.text: Fault 2 · Picked window "Arrivals up 37% in a year" As published: two months of thirty-six. Repaired: every month. October 2024 was the first Honey Festival. The typical yearly growth is about 7%. Ask of any two-point comparison: why these two points?

slides.title: "The Cable Car is our problem site"
slides.text: Fault 3 · Count for rate "The Cable Car is our problem site" As published: complaints. Repaired: per thousand visitors. The picture of yesterday's lab 2.2: the busiest site leads any count. The repair changes the measure, not the drawing.

slides.title: "Hotels follow the sites exactly"
slides.text: Fault 4 · Two axes "Hotels follow the sites exactly" As published: two y axes, each fitted to its line. Repaired: one variable against the other. With two free axes, any two series can be made to overlap. Where they cross means nothing. The scatter shows the relation at its true strength: 0.70, loosely.

slides.title: "Local visits keep climbing"
slides.text: Fault 5 · Running total "Local visits keep climbing" As published: arrivals since January 2023. Repaired: arrivals per month. A running total rises whenever anything arrives at all. It cannot show a fall. Local arrivals fell 6% over two years: 258,000 in 2023, 242,000 in 2025.

slides.title: "Arrivals fell off a cliff in 2025"
slides.text: Fault 6 · Uneven steps "Arrivals fell off a cliff in 2025" As published: years, a half year and two months. Repaired: three periods of equal length. A year, half a year and a month were drawn as equal steps. Yearly arrivals: 842,000, 914,000, 998,000.

Is it the right measure: rate, per period, per unit? Is there one y axis? Does the title say what the chart shows, and no more? The test of a repair Write what a reader concludes from the chart before and after. If the two sentences agree, the fault was cosmetic. In all six cases here they disagree.

slides.title: The type of the variable chooses the kind of palette
slides.text: Colour is an encoding The type of the variable chooses the kind of palette Categorical Names with no order: origin market, site. Distinct hues of similar weight. Five to seven at most. Sequential Low to high: a count, a rate. One hue from light to dark, as in the heatmap of lab 2.1. Diverging Two directions from a midpoint: above and below a baseline. Two hues meeting in a neutral colour. What goes wrong. A rainbow for a quantity: the eye sees bands where the data has none. Or a light-to-dark ramp for names: the reader sees an order that does not exist.

slides.title: Test the palette for colour-vision deficiency
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 1 Test the palette for colour-vision deficiency Under red-green deficiency the draft's red and green are 7 units apart: hard to tell. The Okabe-Ito palette keeps every pair above 18. Do not trust the look on your own screen.

slides.title: Colour is never the only carrier
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 2 Colour is never the only carrier Safe palette, and a dash pattern per market. A second channel repeats the first: dash for lines, shape for points. Better still, label the lines directly at their ends and drop the legend. The test: print the chart in grey. Can each line still be named?

slides.title: The title states the finding; the rest says how to read it
slides.text: The words on a chart The title states the finding; the rest says how to read it Text Draft Finished Title Arrivals Arrivals grew fastest from the smallest markets Subtitle none Yearly arrivals by origin market, 2023 = 100 y axis index Arrivals, 2023 = 100 Legend origin Origin market A title that names the finding can be checked against the chart. "Arrivals" cannot be wrong, or useful. Units, the base of an index, the period and the source belong on the chart, since charts get copied without their page.

slides.title: The words live in a file; the chart is drawn by one function
slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 3 The words live in a file; the chart is drawn by one function L = U.js("labels.json") # every text, in Arabic and English def chart(data, lang): T = L["text"][lang] # title, subtitle, x, y, legend d = data.assign(origin_label=data["origin"].map(L["origins"]) if lang == "ar" else data["origin"]) return alt.Chart(d).mark_line().encode( x=alt.X("year:O", title=T["x"]), y=alt.Y("index:Q", title=T["y"]), color=alt.Color("origin_label:N", title=T["legend"]), ).properties(title=alt.Title(T["title"], subtitle=T["subtitle"])) The data keeps its own column; the labels are mapped at drawing time. Two charts copied and edited by hand drift apart at the first correction.

slides.text: Lab 3.4, step 4 In Arabic the words move; the data does not The Arabic version, from the same function. Title anchored at the right; y axis on the right. House style of this course: Western digits, and time from left to right, in both versions. Let the text engine shape and order Arabic. Never reverse or reshape strings by hand.

slides.title: "Drop" means "this data cannot tell", not "there is no difference"
slides.text: The sentence that goes in the report "Drop" means "this data cannot tell", not "there is no difference" Not supported "The day of the week makes no difference to satisfaction." Supported "The survey shows no clear difference between weekend and weekday visitors (gap 0.02 point, p about 0.35)." A p-value of 0.35 is the absence of evidence for a difference. It is not evidence of absence. To claim "no difference worth acting on", give the interval of the gap and say what size would matter.

slides.title: Resample the unit that was sampled: here, the week
slides.text: Lab 4.1, steps 4 and 5 Resample the unit that was sampled: here, the week 43,840 hotel-days Forty hotels share one day's weather and one day's ticket total. Days in a week resemble each other. Resampling them as if independent gives an interval far too narrow. 156 weeks One row per week for the whole region. Draw 156 weeks with replacement, recompute the correlation, repeat 5,000 times. k = gen.integers(0, len(x), len(x)) # 156 weeks, drawn with replacement r[i] = np.corrcoef(x[k], y[k])[0, 1] What goes wrong. Counting rows as evidence. The number that matters is how many independent units there are.

slides.title: The correlation is not chance, and still needs a qualifier
slides.text: Lab 4.1, steps 5 and 6 The correlation is not chance, and still needs a qualifier 0.70 weekly tickets and hotel occupancy 0.60 to 0.78 95% bootstrap interval, 156 weeks 0.44 with each calendar month's mean removed The interval stays far from zero: weeks with busy sites do have fuller hotels. Part of the 0.70 is the shared season. What remains is smaller and still positive. Decision: qualify. The check answers "is it chance", never "is it cause".

slides.title: A chance check answers one question out of four
slides.text: Before deciding A chance check answers one question out of four Question Answered by Session Could it be chance? a permutation test or a bootstrap interval this one Is it large enough to matter? the size of the effect, in the units of the decision this one Was it found by searching? counting the comparisons that were made 4.3 Is it the mix, the season or the measure? the checks of Day 2 2.2 to 2.4 The decision carries its reason. "Drop: p about 0.35 and a gap of 0.02." "Qualify: interval 0.60 to 0.78; season raises both."

slides.title: Which procedure, on which unit?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which procedure, on which unit? A school network has test scores of 4,000 pupils in 40 schools. Twenty schools used a new timetable. The analyst wants an interval for the difference in mean score between the two groups of schools. What should be resampled? The 4,000 pupils, drawn again with replacement The timetable labels of the pupils, shuffled The 4,000 scores, drawn within each school The 40 schools, drawn again with replacement

slides.title: Showing uncertainty
slides.text: Session 2 Showing uncertainty Add an interval to every estimate on a chart Read overlapping and separate intervals without overclaiming Write a caption that names the interval, the sample size and the limit 02

slides.title: "Terrace Farms is our best-rated site"
slides.text: The earlier report "Terrace Farms is our best-rated site" As published: mean satisfaction in 2025. Each bar is one number drawn as if it were exact. The bars rest on 59 to 510 responses. The chart does not say which. And yesterday's fault 1: bars on an axis from 3.8.

slides.title: Every estimate on a chart gets an interval
slides.text: Lab 4.2, steps 1 and 2 Every estimate on a chart gets an interval Site Responses Mean 95% interval Terrace Farms 59 4.24 4.02 to 4.44 Souq Walk 442 4.22 4.13 to 4.30 Honey Museum 167 4.10 3.97 to 4.24 Cable Car 510 3.93 3.84 to 4.00 Wadi Trail 132 3.91 3.76 to 4.05 The fewer the responses, the wider the interval: roughly with one over the square root of n. The site at the top has the widest interval of all.

slides.title: A point, a line for the interval, and n beside the name
slides.text: Lab 4.2, step 3 A point, a line for the interval, and n beside the name Mean satisfaction in 2025 with 95% bootstrap intervals. A point is read by position, so the axis may run from 3.6 to 4.6. Seven of the other eight intervals overlap that of Terrace Farms.

slides.title: Overlap does not prove equality: compute the interval of the difference
slides.text: Lab 4.2, step 4 Overlap does not prove equality: compute the interval of the difference Two intervals that do not overlap: the groups differ. Two intervals that overlap: this sample cannot order them. They may still differ. For a claim about two groups, resample both and take the difference each time. Guided against unguided visits, 2025 Difference in mean satisfaction: +0.39 point, interval +0.31 to +0.47, from 680 guided and 1,520 unguided responses. The whole interval is far above zero: report. What goes wrong. Reading "overlapping" as "the same" and announcing that all sites perform equally.

slides.title: Uncertainty has its own marks
slides.text: Which mark for which chart Uncertainty has its own marks Point and interval For a few estimates by group. The default of this course. Band around a line For an estimate over time: a shaded band from the lower to the upper end at each date. The data itself With small groups, draw every value as a faint point behind the estimate. Twelve points say "twelve" better than any interval. Avoid a bar with a whisker on top: the bar still says "this much from zero", and readers judge by the bar. And never draw an interval without saying what it is.

slides.title: The caption names the interval, the sample and the limit
slides.text: Lab 4.2, step 5 The caption names the interval, the sample and the limit As publishedTerrace Farms is our best-rated site. RewrittenMean satisfaction in 2025 by site with 95% bootstrap intervals. The Souq Walk (4.22, n = 442) rates above the Cable Car (3.93, n = 510); Terrace Farms' 4.24 rests on 59 responses and cannot be ranked first. The intervals show how far each mean could move with another sample of respondents; they do not correct for who chose to answer or for the mix of visitors at each site. An interval covers sampling variation only. Who answers a survey, how the question is put and the mix of visitors are outside it.

slides.title: What may the report say?
slides.text: Checkpoint What may the report say? Two call centres have mean satisfaction 4.3 (interval 4.1 to 4.5, n = 80) and 4.1 (interval 4.0 to 4.2, n = 600). The intervals overlap. Which statement is supported? The two centres deliver the same level of satisfaction This sample cannot rank them; the difference needs its own interval The first centre is better, since its mean is higher The second centre is better, since its interval is narrower

slides.title: The traps of exploring
slides.text: Session 3 The traps of exploring Count the comparisons behind a reported pattern Simulate the most striking gap that chance alone produces among that many comparisons Mark a finding exploratory or confirmed and name the check it needs 03

slides.title: "At the Honey Museum, weekend visitors were far more satisfied in 2025"
slides.text: A week after the weekend claim was dropped "At the Honey Museum, weekend visitors were far more satisfied in 2025" +0.30 weekend minus weekday, on a 1 to 5 scale 0.03 p-value by permutation, taken alone 167 responses: 68 weekend, 99 weekday Fourteen times the gap that was dropped this morning. It passes a chance check. It is large enough to matter. One question is left: how was it found?

slides.title: It was the most striking of 27 comparisons
slides.text: Lab 4.3, step 2 It was the most striking of 27 comparisons Nine sites, three years: 27 gaps were looked at. One was kept. 16 are above zero, 11 below.

slides.title: With 27 comparisons of nothing, a "finding" is the likely outcome
slides.text: Lab 4.3, step 3 With 27 comparisons of nothing, a "finding" is the likely outcome 1 comparison 1 - 0.95^1 = 5% 5 comparisons 1 - 0.95^5 = 23% 27 comparisons 1 - 0.95^27 = 75% 135 comparisons 1 - 0.95^135 = 99.9% A p-value of 0.05 means: one time in twenty, nothing looks like something. Look twenty-seven times and it is three chances in four. 135 is what the search becomes if it also splits by origin market.

slides.title: Check the method that was used, search included
slides.text: Lab 4.3, step 4 Check the method that was used, search included The most striking of 27 gaps when the labels mean nothing. Shuffle the weekend labels inside every site and year; keep the most striking of the 27 gaps; repeat. Its median is 2.3 standard errors. The headline's is 2.2. A gap as striking as the headline turns up in about half of the shuffles.

slides.title: Every choice made after looking is a comparison
slides.text: Beyond 27 Every choice made after looking is a comparison Which groups: weekend, or Friday alone, or school holidays? Which measure: the mean, or the share of 5s? Which rows: all responses, or "excluding" a bad month? Which period: 2025, or the last six months? In the board's past report "Visitors who arrive on a Tuesday spend the most": spend tabulated by every day of the week, every origin and every purpose, and the largest cell reported. No bad faith is needed. An honest analyst who looks until something stands out has run many tests and remembers one.

slides.title: What makes a finding confirmed is the order of events
slides.text: Lab 4.3, step 5 What makes a finding confirmed is the order of events Confirmed The question was written down before the data that answers it was looked at. "Guided visits are rated higher": noticed in the 2023 survey, written down, then tested once on the 2024 survey. Exploratory The data suggested the question. "Hotels in the Ridge zone fill up before the Honey Festival": seen in a chart of 2024 while looking for something else. Exploratory is a label, not an insult: it is where questions come from. The same data cannot both suggest a pattern and confirm it.

slides.title: An exploratory finding is reported with its count and its next test
slides.text: Lab 4.3, step 6 An exploratory finding is reported with its count and its next test 1 · Label "Exploratory", in the sentence itself → 2 · Count how many comparisons it was chosen from → 3 · Write down the question, before new data exists → 4 · Test once on data that did not suggest it In the report. "Exploratory: among 27 comparisons, the most striking gap was 0.30 point at the Honey Museum in 2025; shuffled labels produce one as striking about half the time. The question will be tested once on the 2026 survey."

slides.title: What is this finding worth?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is this finding worth? An analyst compares churn between customers who did and did not use each of 40 app features. One feature shows a difference with p = 0.02. The team wants to announce "Feature X reduces churn". What should the analyst say? It is exploratory: expected among 40 looks; test it once on new customers It is confirmed, because the p-value is well below 0.05 It will be confirmed once the test is rerun with more shuffles It should be discarded and left out of the report entirely

slides.title: A report that reruns
slides.text: Session 4 A report that reruns Render a report from raw data with one command and prove that two runs agree Find what makes a report change between runs Write findings with their check, their limit and an open question 04

slides.title: A report that reruns has one path from the raw data to the page
slides.text: The promise A report that reruns has one path from the raw data to the page Raw data read-only, never edited by hand → One source text and code together, parameters at the top → One command runs everything in a fresh process → The page every number computed by that run No number is typed; no chart is pasted. A correction to the data reaches every figure at the next render. Somebody else can run it and get the same page.

slides.title: Render twice and compare: the first test of any report
slides.text: Lab 4.4, steps 1 and 2 Render twice and compare: the first test of any report first render : out/draft_a.html, digest 27942ef6cebc second render: out/draft_b.html, digest 319a4f665407 correlation_high: 0.783 then 0.78 correlation_low: 0.602 then 0.6 Nothing was changed between the two runs. The bootstrap drew different resamples. A fixed seed, passed as a parameter, makes two runs agree. A third decimal is enough for two people to hold two versions of "the" report.

slides.title: A cached number is a number with no code behind it
slides.text: Lab 4.4, step 3 A cached number is a number with no code behind it In the report From the cache From the raw data Stays 40,600 40,000 Stays from the Gulf 5,553 6,063 Mean length of stay, nights 11.27 3.30 The summary was saved once, before lab 1.2 found the duplicate rows, the 999 nights and the three spellings of "Gulf". It was right on the day it was saved. Later decisions about the data never reached it.

slides.title: Every finding carries its status, its check and its limit
slides.text: Lab 4.4, step 4 Every finding carries its status, its check and its limit Finding Status Check Limit Weeks with more ticket sales are weeks with fuller hotels (0.70) exploratory bootstrap of 156 weeks: 0.60 to 0.78 season raises both; no causal claim Guided visits were rated 0.4 point higher in 2025 confirmed question written before the 2024 survey was opened visitors choose a guided visit Weekend gap at the Honey Museum (0.30) exploratory most striking of 27; as striking in half of shuffles to be tested on the 2026 survey The table is the report's spine. A reader with two minutes reads it and nothing else, so no finding may sit in it without a limit.

slides.title: An exploratory report says what was seen, how sure, and what is still open
slides.text: The reader is not an analyst An exploratory report says what was seen, how sure, and what is still open Findings first , each one sentence with its number, in the reader's words. One chart per finding , titled with the finding, drawn with its uncertainty. Open questions : what the data suggested and has not tested. Limits : what the data cannot show, and who is missing from it. Words to keep out "Proves", "causes", "significant" with no number, "the data says". An exploratory report writes "we saw", "in this data", "to be tested".
